title: From the end
hookLine: decide one thing by what you'd value on your last day

cards: Two options on the kitchen table. Maybe two jobs, or two weekends, or one hard phone call you keep moving to next week. You've made the list of pros and cons, and the columns come out even.
You've asked three friends and gotten three answers. Some decisions just sit there, refusing to tip.

Ignatius of Loyola, the founder of the Jesuits, wrote a small book of prayer exercises, and tucked inside it is a strange tool for exactly this moment. It asks you to stand somewhere else before you choose.

teach.b: First, a book for choosing. The Spiritual Exercises are a set of prayers and meditations, and part of the book is about making a choice, which Ignatius calls an election. He doesn't offer one method.
He offers several, for different kinds of moments, including the moments when nothing seems clear.

Second, stand at the end. One of his ways, in plain paraphrase: consider, as if you were at the point of death, what way of deciding this present matter you would then wish you had chosen, and choose that way now.
It's a change of seat. Instead of what you want this week, you ask what you'd be glad of from the last chair. Third, a neighbor's tool.
In the same few lines Ignatius offers a cousin of it: picture a person you've never met who brings you this exact choice, notice what you'd advise them, and take your own advice.
Both tools step you out of the knot, so the choice can be seen whole. Fourth, the setting.
For Ignatius, this happens inside prayer, as a way of seeking what God wants, and Jesuits and others who give the Exercises still teach it that way.
People outside that faith sometimes borrow its shape as a quiet thinking tool.
Either way, the question is surprisingly practical: from the end, which of these will I be glad I chose?

how: In Ignatian retreats and spiritual direction, a person facing a decision may be guided to consider, in prayer, what they would wish they had chosen at the point of death; others use the same question informally when making choices.

o: the Jesuit founder whose Exercises include choosing from the end
a desert monk who taught silence as the way to choose
a Jesuit scholar who wrote a well-known guide to wills

games.q: what's inside Ignatius's tool — tap the pairs.
p: consider it as if at death

s: Ignatius offers only one way to make a choice
he offers several, for different kinds of moments.
one of his ways is to consider the choice as if at the point of death
and then to choose now what you'd then wish you had chosen.
the tool asks you to choose whatever you want most this week
it changes the seat: what would you be glad of from the end?

games.q: your pros and cons come out even. Ignatius has a tool for this. what does it ask?
o: flip a coin and trust it.
consider, as if at death, what you'd wish you had chosen, then choose it.
games.why: Ignatius suggests standing at the point of death in imagination, then choosing now what you'd then be glad of.

practice: Bring one small, real choice to mind, how to spend this evening, whether to send a message, what to say yes to, and hold both options lightly.
Now sit for a moment in that last chair, calm, the day almost done, and look back: which way would you be glad of, without arguing with the answer or forcing one?
If you pray, you can bring the choice into prayer the way Ignatius did; then choose, or simply rest.

wordCard.voice: Ignatius, whose Spiritual Exercises offer a tool: choose as you'd wish you had, seen from your last day. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the last chair. A choice can look different from there. Day eight hundred eight, done.
